CA.name: California
CA.summary: SB 868 (1,200 W AC per dwelling, no utility approval or fees) passed both houses; presented to Gov. Newsom Aug 31, 2026. No action as of Sep 23; deadline Sep 30, 2026.
CA.certification: Certified as a plug-in PV system by UL or equivalent NRTL; UL/NRTL-certified anti-backfeed isolation feature; NEC + California Electrical Code
CA.notes: Official history (fetched 2026-09-23): Senate 35-1 (5/19/26), Assembly 73-0 (8/25/26), Senate concurred 36-4 (8/26/26), enrolled 8/28, presented to Governor 8/31/26; no chapter or veto recorded, and SB 868 is absent from governor releases through 9/22/26. Under Cal. Const. art. IV §10(b)(2) the Governor must act by Sept 30, 2026 or it becomes law without signature; if enacted it takes effect Jan 1, 2027 (art. IV §8(c)(1); no urgency clause). The enrolled text exempts qualifying devices from all interconnection requirements, bars utility approval/fees/extra equipment, allows a simple online registration, sunsets the exemption (PUC §8531) on Jan 1, 2030, and from Jan 1, 2030 bans sale of non-compliant plug-in PV devices (§8532). It has no landlord/tenant/HOA provisions and is silent on export compensation.

CO.name: Colorado
CO.summary: HB26-1007: utilities cannot require approval or fees for plug-in solar up to 1,920 W (in force Aug 12, 2026). Ban on unreasonable landlord/HOA/covenant limits starts Jan 1, 2027.
CO.certification: Labeled and listed by an NRTL. From Jan 1, 2027, devices over 391 W may not be sold, leased or rented unless UL labeled and listed. Must have anti-islanding.
CO.notes: The law adds C.R.S. 40-2-140. A device is a single PV system per address supplying no more than 1,920 W to the grid. The text states this as output to the grid and does not explicitly say inverter AC rating. It is limited to one device per wall outlet per address. Utilities may not require approval, fees or extra equipment, but may require notice of the device's presence and size. Devices of 391 W or less are exempt from 40-2-128 installer requirements and from code or listing provisions requiring wiring changes. The act does not address net metering or export credit. On the effective date, trackers said Aug 12, 2026 or Jan 1, 2027. Section 6 of the signed act sets 90 days after sine die (Aug 12, 2026; the 2026 session ended May 13), and the bill page lists Session Law ch. 127 effective 08/12/2026. However, §40-2-140(6)-(7) apply only 'on and after January 1, 2027': the UL sales rule, the ban on unreasonable prohibitions (void covenants, HOA energy-efficiency-measure treatment including limited common element balconies) and reasonable owner restrictions. So the tenant and HOA right to install is enacted but not yet operative.

CT.name: Connecticut
CT.summary: Public Act 26-127 (HB 5340) sec. 9 exempts one plug-in solar device of up to 1,200 W per meter from interconnection, utility approval and fees. Takes effect Oct 1, 2026.
CT.certification: Certified by UL or an equivalent NRTL and meets UL 1741; meets IEEE 1547, NEC (NFPA 70) and State Building Code; must have anti-islanding
CT.notes: Sec. 9 of PA 26-127 (marked 'Effective October 1, 2026') covers a 'portable solar generation device': not permanently affixed, max power output of 1,200 W or less, plugs into a 120 V outlet behind the meter. It is exempt from PURA interconnection requirements, but only one device is allowed behind each meter, and utilities cannot require approval, fees or extra equipment. The device must carry a warning that generation beyond on-site use is charged to the customer as usage unless the customer has a net-metering meter, so exports are not credited by default. The act gives no landlord, tenant or HOA right. It says the device stays subject to the State Building Code, Fire Safety Code and local ordinances. Sec. 10 asks code officials to consider plug-in provisions in their next updates. The statute says 'maximum power output', not specifically AC inverter output. The 2026 regular session ended May 6, 2026. The Oct 1, 2026 date and June 4, 2026 signing in trackers match the act; no conflicts found.

IL.name: Illinois
IL.summary: SB 3104 passed Senate committee but was re-referred to Assignments on May 22, 2026. The 104th GA runs until January 2027, so it could technically still move, but it has stalled.
IL.certification: Proposed: UL or equivalent NRTL certification (SB 3104 as amended)
IL.notes: The official status page (Wayback snapshot of ILGA, 2026-06-15) shows Senate Committee Amendments 2 and 3 adopted and 'Do Pass as Amended' out of Energy and Public Utilities (9-4) on 3/12/2026. The bill then reached 2nd reading but never got a floor vote. Its last action on 5/22/2026 was 'Rule 3-9(a) / Re-referred to Assignments'. As amended, SB 3104 makes devices not eligible for net metering or DG rebates and requires owners to notify their utility within 30 days. It bars HOAs and landlords from unreasonably restricting installation. It exempts systems of 391 W or less from code or listing rules that would require wiring or panel alterations, and it prohibits systems over 391 W until the NEC adopts a standard, so the working cap is 391 W. House companion HB 4524 (1,200 W export cap, landlord/HOA protections) was re-referred to Rules on 3/27/2026. The 104th GA lasts until the 105th is seated in January 2027, and fall veto or lame-duck days remain. Moving the bill would need Assignments to release it and both chambers to pass it. The sponsor said she will pursue it in 2027 (NPR Illinois), and trackers already call it dead or deferred. ILGA was unreachable from this environment, so statuses rely on June 2026 Wayback snapshots of the official pages. Cap/certification/right fields describe the bill's last version, not law.

ME.name: Maine
ME.summary: LD 1730 (Public Law ch. 644) allows plug-in solar up to 420 W DIY, or up to 1,200 W with a licensed electrician and utility notice. No interconnection; no net energy billing. In force July 29, 2026.
ME.certification: Listed or certified to UL 3700, or a comparable NRTL standard, or configured per the NEC adopted by the Electricians' Examining Board. Inverters must shut off within 0.2 s of a power disruption.
ME.notes: The law enacts 35-A MRSA §3475, which covers plug-in PV and battery systems. Up to 420 W (combined inverter AC output per service address) needs no electrician and no utility notice. From 420 W to 1,200 W, each system must be installed by a Maine-licensed electrician on a dedicated single-outlet circuit, and the customer must notify the utility within 30 days. Utilities may not require approval, an interconnection application or agreement, fees or extra equipment. Eligible systems 'may not be used for net energy billing'. The law creates no landlord or HOA right to install: subsection 8 only requires a customer on a structure they do not own to protect its integrity, follow building, fire and zoning codes, and restore it on removal. On the effective date, trackers said July 14 or 15, 2026. The chapter law has no emergency clause, and the Legislature's site states the general effective date for non-emergency 2nd Regular Session laws is July 29, 2026 (90 days after the April 29, 2026 sine die, Me. Const. art. IV, pt. 3, §16), so we used July 29. The bill's original title was 'An Act Regarding the Beneficial Electrification Policy of the State' before it was retitled.

MD.name: Maryland
MD.summary: Utility RELIEF Act (HB 1532, Ch. 353) adds PUA §7-321: one plug-in system up to 1,200 W per meter, no utility approval or fee, notice before install. Effective July 1, 2026.
MD.certification: Certified by UL or an equivalent NRTL. Devices of 391 W or less are exempt from listing provisions that would require premises, wiring or panel alterations.
MD.notes: Plug-in solar is one section of a 244-page omnibus energy act; there is no separate cross-filed plug-in bill. It sits in Section 4 of the act as new Public Utilities Art. §7-321. The device must be moveable, plug into a standard outlet and supply no more than 1,200 W back to the building's electric system, limited to one per meter for residential use only. Utilities may not require approval, feed-in fees or extra equipment. The customer must notify the utility before installing, provide a certification of safety features and capacity, and pay for an automatic locking disconnect if one is required. Devices are not subject to §7-306 (net metering) or §7-306.1 (interconnection agreements), do not count toward the RPS and may not generate RECs. The act has no landlord, tenant or HOA provision. On the effective date, trackers said May 12, 2026 (immediately) or Oct 1, 2026. The act is an emergency measure effective on enactment (May 12, 2026) except the sections listed in its Section 22, which include Section 4 and take effect July 1, 2026. The DLS Fiscal and Policy Note (Enrolled-Revised) confirms 'Effective Date: July 1, 2026' for this provision, so both tracker dates are wrong for plug-in solar. The standalone 'Affordable Solar Act' bills (HB 345/SB 341), which also had portable-solar language, got committee hearings only and died when the session ended.

NH.name: New Hampshire
NH.summary: SB 540 (Chapter 262, signed July 2, 2026) lets each metered customer run one plug-in solar system up to 1,200 W AC without utility approval or interconnection. Takes effect Jan 1, 2027.
NH.certification: Certified by an NRTL to nationally recognized safety standards for DER and plug-in systems; must meet national interconnection and interoperability standards (IEEE 1547 implied, not named)
NH.notes: Chaptered text (Ch. 262, 'Approved: July 02, 2026') sec. 262:7 makes everything except sec. 3 effective January 1, 2027. Sec. 3, the building-code provision (RSA 155-A:16), takes effect only once the Dept. of Energy commissioner certifies that a nationally recognized plug-in standard exists. This settles the tracker conflicts: 'effective Jul 27, 2026' and 'remainder took effect July 2, 2026' are wrong, and so are 'Chapter 89' and a July 9 signing date. RSA 362-A:10 allows one system of up to 1,200 W AC per metered customer. Utilities cannot require approval, interconnection review or agreement, fees or extra equipment, and may only ask for notification of the wattage. The law does not say whether exports are credited. RSA 374:1-b says utilities are not liable for 'compensation or charges arising from' a plug-in system, which suggests no credit but does not say so outright. There are no landlord, HOA or local-government provisions. The 2026 session has ended.

NJ.name: New Jersey
NJ.summary: Garden State Balcony Solar Act (P.L.2026, c.82): plug-in solar up to 1,200 W, no interconnection; landlords, HOAs and towns can't ban it. Signed Sept 1, 2026; effective Mar 1, 2027.
NJ.certification: Listed or certified by an NRTL to UL 3700 or a comparable standard or combination of standards; anti-islanding; installed per product listing, NEC and UCC
NJ.notes: P.L.2026, c.82 (approved 9/1/2026) takes effect 'six months after the date of enactment', i.e. March 1, 2027; the BPU may act in advance. This matches trackers. Devices of up to 1,200 W (combined per service address, or per dwelling unit in multifamily housing) are exempt from interconnection agreements and net-metering program requirements. Utilities cannot require approval, fees or extra equipment. The act does not say whether exported energy is compensated. Devices of 400 W or less are exempt from listing and code provisions that would require wiring or panel alterations. Landlords cannot bar tenants who pay their own electric bill from using a device within their leased premises, including a balcony or patio; reasonable size and placement limits are allowed and tenants must give 14 days' written notice. HOAs and condos cannot enforce bans on exterior placement. Municipalities cannot prohibit the devices or require permits.

UT.name: Utah
UT.summary: HB 340 (2025) exempts plug-in solar up to 1,200 W from utility interconnection, approval and fees. In force since May 7, 2025. Not part of net metering; no tenant or HOA rights.
UT.certification: Certified by UL or an equivalent NRTL, must meet the current NEC, and must have anti-islanding (cannot energize the building during an outage)
UT.notes: The official title is 'Solar Power Amendments', not 'Consumer Electricity Amendments' as the lead said. It enacts Utah Code 54-15-601 and amends 54-15-102. A 'portable solar generation device' is a moveable PV device with maximum power output of 1,200 W or less that plugs into a standard 120 V outlet. The statute does not say whether that figure is AC or DC. The device is exempt from interconnection requirements and interconnection agreements and 'is not subject to the net metering program requirements'. It is also excluded from the definition of a customer generation system, so exports earn no net-metering credit. Utilities may not require approval, fees or extra equipment, and they are not liable for damage. There is no landlord, tenant, HOA or local-government provision. The enrolled text sets the effective date as May 7, 2025, matching the trackers. The 2026 General Session has ended, and le.utah.gov still lists the 2025 version of 54-15-601 as the only current version, so nothing amended it in 2026.

VT.summary: Act 149 (S.202), in force July 1, 2026: plug-in PV up to 1,200 W combined per meter, UL 3700, smart meter required, no interconnection, no export credit; renter, HOA and zoning protections.
VT.certification: UL 3700 (or equivalent NRTL certification); installed and operated per IEEE 1547-2018 with default regional profiles; anti-islanding; smart meter required
VT.notes: Under 30 V.S.A. sec. 256, a customer may install one or more plug-in devices per meter, up to 1,200 W combined inverter capacity. Devices may only connect to smart-metered systems and must be temporarily but securely attached. They are exempt from sec. 248 CPG, interconnection agreements and PUC jurisdiction. Utilities cannot require approval, installation fees or extra equipment, but may recover costs if the device overloads the service. Net-metering customers cannot also install one, the device is not eligible for net metering, and exports are expressly uncompensated. Tenants must give the landlord 10 days' notice. The landlord may impose reasonable restrictions (e.g. a licensed electrician at the tenant's cost); if the landlord does not respond, the tenant may proceed. Deed restrictions and covenants (including condo patio-railing rules) cannot prohibit plug-in devices, and zoning bylaws may not regulate them. No source conflicts found.

VA.name: Virginia
VA.summary: HB 395/SB 250 (Chs. 1052/998): plug-in solar up to 1,200 W is exempt from interconnection; utility notice before install; tenant and locality protections. Takes effect Jan 1, 2027.
VA.certification: Certified by an NRTL (29 CFR 1910.7) or equivalent, must meet the current NEC, and must have anti-islanding. Devices of 391 W or less are exempt from listing provisions that would require wiring or panel alterations.
VA.notes: The identical chaptered acts (HB 395 = Ch. 1052, SB 250 = Ch. 998, both approved Apr 22, 2026 at the reconvened session) add Va. Code §56-596.8 (numbered §56-596.7 in the chaptered acts) and §55.1-1212.1 and amend §15.2-2288.7, §56-594 and related sections. Devices are excluded from net energy metering and from the definition of eligible customer-generator. Utilities may not require approval or fees, but the customer must file an SCC notification form before installing. The utility has 15 days to respond, and utilities may install a locking disconnect in some cases. Landlords owning more than 4 units may not prohibit tenants from installing on the exterior of the tenant's premises (reasonable size, place and manner limits allowed; 7 days' notice required; excludes RUBS-billed units). Localities may not prohibit devices on residential structures. HOA, condo and POA covenants are expressly NOT overridden. On the effective date, trackers said July 1, 2026 or Jan 1, 2027. Enactment clause 4 makes the first enactment (all Code changes) effective Jan 1, 2027. Enactments 2-3 (the SCC form due Sept 1, 2026 and a safety work group) take the default July 1, 2026 date (Va. Const. art. IV §13). So both tracker dates are partly right, but the device rights do not start until Jan 1, 2027.

WA.name: Washington
WA.summary: SSB 6050 (1,200 W, UL 3700) died in Senate Rules. Companion HB 2296 became law (ch. 136, 2026) but only after its plug-in solar provisions were removed.
WA.certification: Proposed only (SSB 6050): UL 3700; UL 1741 or IEEE 1547 anti-islanding; UL 3141 if paired with storage
WA.notes: SSB 6050 got a do-pass from Senate ENET on 1/30/2026 and was sent to Rules on 2/2. It went to the Senate Rules 'X' file on 2/26/2026, its last action. The session ended on March 12, 2026, which closed the 2025-26 biennium. The bill would have exempted devices from interconnection and net metering after the customer notified the utility, and barred utilities, cities, counties and landlords from requiring approval or fees. It would have stopped HOA and condo documents from prohibiting devices, but utilities with fewer than 25,000 customers could ban them. HB 2296 as introduced had a balcony-solar part, but the House substitute that passed 56-38 covered only meter-mounted devices. The Senate then rewrote it into rental energy-efficiency financing, enacted as ch. 136, Laws of 2026 (signed 3/23/2026, effective 6/11/2026), with no plug-in provisions. Conflict: one secondary source says the House passed HB 2296 with plug-in provisions, but the official substitute text contradicts that. Cap/certification/right fields describe the bill's last version, not law.

WV.name: West Virginia
WV.summary: HB 5648 (2026) would have exempted ≤1,200 W certified portable solar from interconnection (no net metering); it died in committee when the session ended March 14, 2026.
WV.certification: UL or other nationally recognized testing laboratory (as proposed)
WV.notes: HB 5648 (Del. Eldridge) was an omnibus utility-consumer bill whose proposed §24-2F-1 defined a 'portable solar generation device' (outlet-connected, max output 1,200 W — introduced text literally reads '1.200 watts'), exempted it from interconnection agreements, made it ineligible for net metering, and barred utilities from requiring approval, fees or extra equipment; it had no landlord/HOA/tenant provisions. It was referred to House Energy and Public Works, a motion to discharge was tabled 3/2/2026 (Roll 230), and it died when the Legislature adjourned sine die March 14, 2026. Conflict: Bright Saver, PlugInSolarMap and a June 2026 guide say WV has no plug-in bill — they missed this generically titled bill; resolved from the legislature's bill text and history. No plug-in law is in force; any successor must be filed in the 2027 session.

The 2025–26 session's last general-business floor period ended March 19, 2026, so nothing can move before 2027.

WY.name: Wyoming
WY.summary: HB 146 ('Affordable electricity act', 1,200 W per meter) died in House committee on Mar 3, 2026, during the budget session.
WY.certification: Proposed only: UL or equivalent NRTL certification plus current NEC; outage anti-backfeed
WY.notes: The official LSO record shows HB 146 (Rep. Storer et al.) introduced on 2/11/2026 on a 55-5 vote and referred to House committee H08. It got 'No report prior to CoW Cutoff' on 2/20/2026 and 'Died in Committee Returned Bill Pursuant to HR 5-4' on 3/3/2026; the record's status is 'inactive'. The bill would have exempted 1,200 W-per-meter devices from interconnection and net-metering requirements and barred utility approval or fees. It would have let utilities offer bidirectional meters and would have taken effect July 1, 2026. It had no landlord or HOA provisions. The budget session adjourned sine die on March 11, 2026. Conflict: pluginsolarmap says 'no bill filed yet', which is wrong. Cap/certification/right fields describe the bill's last version, not law.
